argument: Where existentialists like Sartre, Kierkegaard, and Heidegger explain despair, anxiety, and nausea by a lack of something, Ernst Bloch's early work explains the same experiences by a surplus of hope, or anticipatory consciousness. For Bloch hope is an ontological category, the dynamic of being itself: consciousness and the world co-constitute each other and are both oriented toward the Not-Yet, so no lived moment can be grasped in full. This reframing turns existential crisis into unrealized anticipatory energy, cynicism into Bloch's version of philosophical suicide, and disappointment into a moment of recalibration, while his four filters of educated hope separate futures rooted in real historical potential from wishful thinking.
keyIdeas: Bloch answers the existentialists' questions by explaining difficult experiences through a surplus of hope, or anticipatory consciousness, rather than a lack of essence, certainty, or ground.
Hope is ontological, not psychological: it is the dynamic of being itself, with the world as well as people oriented toward the Not-Yet, so that even a stone is becoming world.
Because the world is incomplete and we are unfinished and too close to ourselves, we live in the darkness of the lived moment, and every moment carries latent future possibilities.

Anxiety and nihilism are surplus phenomena: doing nothing leaves unrealized anticipatory energy, and cynicism, Bloch's equivalent of philosophical suicide, is usually a retreat after hope was disappointed by an inaccurate picture of the future.

Hope shows up everywhere in culture, from music's tension and resolution to superhero movies as wish landscapes, and educated hope must pass the filters of tendency, latency, mobilization, and revision.

terms.def: Bloch's name for hope as the core of what we are: consciousness rooted in time, constantly oriented toward future possibilities and co-evolving with the world.
The future worlds and latent possibilities that haven't been brought about, toward which both consciousness and the world itself are always oriented.
The blind spot of the present: the world and ourselves are incomplete and too close to us for any moment to be grasped in full.
Hope rooted in the actual conditions of the world rather than fantasy, tested by the four filters of tendency, latency, mobilization, and revision.
Bloch's idea that no artwork is totally random; every piece at least subtly reflects what the artist feels is missing in the present or possible in the future.
Seeing people who disagree with you not as less developed but as occupying different moments in the history of ideas, living together at the same time.
